items.prose: The fifty-meter-deep detonation crater filled with groundwater, forming a permanently stratified meromictic lake. Below fifteen meters, the monimolimnion water is completely anoxic, pitch black, and saturated with 240 ppm dissolved hydrogen sulfide gas that preserves organic matter without rotting.

Sediment cores retrieved from the lake center show a sixty-centimeter layer of jet-black sapropel mud. Heavy metals leached from industrial wreckage (lead, cadmium, arsenic) precipitate as insoluble sulfides, locking toxins in the sediment unless disturbed by dredging.

During summer months, the warm epilimnion layer (0-5m) is blanketed by a dense scum of radiotrophic blue-green cyanobacteria (*Microcystis radiata*). The algae produce lethal concentrations of hepatotoxic microcystin; drinking unfiltered lake water causes acute hepatic necrosis within twelve hours.

A razor-sharp thermocline at eight meters depth acts as a density barrier. Dissolved strontium-90 washed in from surface fallout is trapped in the cold hypolimnion (4°C), leaving the warm surface water relatively low in radiation but biologically toxic.

An intense autumn cold snap cooled the lake surface to 2°C, causing sudden density overturn of the water column. Over twelve hundred tons of dissolved carbon dioxide and methane erupted as a massive silent gas cloud, asphyxiating wildlife and scouts along the shoreline for two miles.

Alkaline concrete leachate raised lake pH to 9.8, triggering a spontaneous precipitation event of microcrystalline calcium carbonate. The water turned an opaque, milky turquoise for three weeks, neutralizing dissolved heavy metals and settling radioactive dust out of suspension.

The central rebound peak of the nuclear crater forms a steep, conical island rising six meters above the lake surface. Isolated by toxic deep water, the island is covered with hundreds of nests of two-headed cormorants, whose guano forms an acidic phosphorus-rich crust.
